title: Daily decrease
hookLine: learning adds every day; the Tao subtracts every day (Tao Te Ching 48)

lines: AN ELEPHANT FROM A BLOCK OF STONE.
cards: How does a sculptor make an elephant out of a block of stone? The old joke answer: cut away everything that doesn't look like an elephant. It gets a laugh because it turns making things backward.
Usually people add. They stack, collect, sign up, learn one more thing.
Chapter forty-eight of the Tao Te Ching sets those two motions side by side, adding and taking away, and gives each one to a different kind of person.

teach.b: In James Legge's translation: "He who devotes himself to learning (seeks) from day to day to increase (his knowledge); he who devotes himself to the Tao (seeks) from day to day to diminish (his doing)." Learning adds.
The way subtracts. Second, what the chapter doesn't say. It doesn't call learning bad.
It describes two motions with two aims.

teach.h: CLEARING THE FLOOR, NOT THE SHELVES.
teach.b: Learning fills the shelves; the way clears the floor. Legge's bracket says what gets cleared: doing. The busy pushing, the extra effort, the noise of trying too hard.
You lessen and lessen again, the chapter says, until you arrive at not forcing anything. Then it echoes chapter thirty-seven: when nothing is forced, nothing is left undone.
And it adds that the world is won by not meddling, and lost by too much busyness.
Fourth, the list. To-do lists tend to grow.
A daily decrease turns the list over. What could come off today? One app you open without thinking.
One commitment you said yes to out of guilt. One habit of explaining yourself over and over. One object that only collects dust.
The way, in this chapter, isn't reached by adding a new practice on top of everything else. It's reached by setting something down, and then, tomorrow, setting down one more.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-eight as a call to simplify, letting go of one habit, possession or effort at a time rather than adding new ones.

o: learning one new fact or skill every single day
a slow decline in health that comes with age
the way of setting a little more down each day

s: chapter forty-eight says learning is bad
it describes two motions with two aims: learning adds, the way subtracts.
in Legge's bracket, what the way diminishes is doing
the extra effort and pushing, not knowledge itself.
the chapter says the world is won by being as busy as possible
it says the world is won by not meddling.

games.q: you want to grow on the way, and your week is already full. what does chapter forty-eight suggest?
o: add a new practice on top of everything.
take one thing away, then another.
learn more about the way first.
games.why: the chapter says the one devoted to the way diminishes from day to day, lessening and lessening again.

practice: Breathe out a little longer than you breathe in, and with each long out-breath let one thing go: the tension in your jaw, the grip in your hands, the plan you were rehearsing. Lessen, and lessen again.
Near the end, let one thing from your actual day come to mind that could simply be dropped, and notice how it feels to set it down.

wordCard.voice: Daily decrease. Chapter forty-eight: learning adds every day, and the way subtracts every day, until nothing is forced. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: to decrease, to lessen; in chapter forty-eight, what the way does day by day.

carryVoice: Your line: less each day. Space is made by setting things down. Rest well.
